summary:
Aguascalientes stands under Mexico's national framework, and legal gender recognition in Mexico is settled state by state. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state survey of 11 March 2025 records that Aguascalientes 'has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people'; its reporting of 31 March 2025 places the state among those that have not legislated such a procedure. The state therefore operates no administrative mechanism of its own for changing name or gender markers on official records.

The March 2024 Human Rights Watch report on the cost of absent recognition names Aguascalientes among the non-reforming states whose trans residents have no lawful marker procedure. Its documented consequence is that trans people carry documents contradicting their lived identity, which amplifies discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

A court-ordered route now exists. Infobae reported on 9 April 2026 that the Supreme Court, in Amparo en Revisión 430/2025 on a draft by Minister Giovanni Figueroa Mejía, held that the state Civil Code's requirements for changing the gender on a birth certificate, namely judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations, are discriminatory and violate privacy. The Court ordered the Civil Registry to grant recognition through a simple, confidential administrative procedure honouring self-perception, issuing a new birth certificate with no marginal note revealing a prior gender. The immediate effect is confined to the persons represented by the civil association that brought the case, so the ruling establishes a recognition route in the absence of legislative reform without yet establishing one for the state's trans population generally.

No trans-specific homicide offence covers the state. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that Mexico City criminalised transfemicide; Aguascalientes is among the states that have adopted no comparable reform.

Violence and coercive practice persist according to local accounts. La Jornada Aguascalientes reported on 23 August 2026 that activists Alicia Cruz, Kevin Cruz and Hened Musalem of Diversx Laboratorio Cultural Disidente say conversion-therapy operations continue in the state under the guise of addiction-treatment annexes despite the legal prohibition, and that a person who escaped one such space reached the group the previous year. The same activists state that trans women continue to suffer prejudice-motivated aggression.
tangentialFactors:
ENDISEG records that 7.3% of Aguascalientes residents aged 15 and over self-identify as LGBTI+, the fifth-highest share among Mexico's states. The figure is a self-identification share, not a count of trans residents.

Recognition in Aguascalientes now rests on litigation rather than statute, in contrast with states that have legislated procedures. The amparo route depends on a civil association's case, while the state legislature has not acted.
localsOnly:
Residents who are not represented by the civil association that brought Amparo en Revisión 430/2025 remain subject to the Civil Code requirements the Supreme Court found discriminatory: judicial or ministerial intervention, a civil trial, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations on the record. Whether the Civil Registry has extended the court-ordered procedure beyond the litigants is not established by the sources.

Conversion therapy is prohibited in Aguascalientes, yet the activists' account places practising operations inside addiction-treatment annexes, with at least one person leaving such a space in the year before August 2026.
outOfScopeNotes:
No state-level count of violence against trans people in Aguascalientes appears in the sources. The activists' account of continuing prejudice-motivated aggression cannot be quantified, and no comparison with the state's general homicide rate can be made from the material available.

Whether the Civil Registry has implemented the April 2026 ruling, and whether the state has issued any general protocol or guidance extending the administrative procedure beyond the represented litigants, is not sourced.

No record of enforcement action under Aguascalientes' prohibition of conversion therapy is available; the sources establish that the practice continues, not that it has been prosecuted.
